subtype: Approach: asking each family member for one wish [Action]
passage: Rukmini Ma'am's homework was to plan a trip that is fair to everybody. Chetan thought of the beach, his favourite. Then he wondered whether Dadi would like a beach. That evening he asked each person one question: "Which one place do you want most?" Dadi said the temple, Mummy the old bookshop, Papa the lighthouse, and his sister the aquarium. Next day in class he showed his chart: four places, each wish with a day beside it, and the beach on the way home as a fifth. "Nobody's wish is left out," he told Rukmini Ma'am, who pinned it on the display board.

qa.q: What was Chetan thinking when he wondered whether Dadi would like a beach?
qa.a: He was thinking of others' tastes, and that a fair plan cannot rest on his own favourite alone.

qa.q: What could Chetan do if two wishes are far apart, and why?
qa.a: He could put them on different days, so nobody spends the whole day travelling between them.

qa.q: How might Chetan's sister feel seeing the aquarium on the chart?
qa.a: She is probably pleased and included, since her wish has a place and a day.

grounding: A boy asks each family member for one wish and builds the trip days around them so nobody feels ignored.

subtype: Approach: asking each family member for one wish [Action]
passage: I'm Alka, Jagdish's sister, and I thought his idea would end in a fight. On our last trip, to Mysore, Papa wanted temples, Mummy wanted silk shops, and Dadi sat in the car sulking. This time Jagdish came round with four chits. "One place each. Anything." Dadi wrote the hill temple. Mummy wrote the silk market. Papa wrote the railway museum, which surprised everyone. I wrote the zoo. Jagdish pinned the chits on the calendar, two for each day, and put his own wish, the palace lights, on Sunday night. On the trip, Dadi prayed a long time on the hill and nobody hurried her. I'm not sure what Jagdish was thinking when Papa laughed at the old engines, but he kept looking round at all of us.

qa.q: What did Papa write on his chit?
What might Jagdish have been feeling when he kept looking round at everyone?
qa.a: He seemed quietly pleased and watchful, perhaps relieved that each person was enjoying their own pick.

qa.q: What else could the family try if two wishes clash on the same day?
qa.a: They could swap the days or take turns choosing the order, keeping the fair idea of one place each.

qa.q: How did the plan look to Dadi this time?
qa.a: Instead of sulking in the car, Dadi got to pray on the hill as long as she liked, with nobody hurrying her.

grounding: A sister watches a boy ask each family member for one place and build the trip days around those choices.

subtype: Approach: asking each family member for one wish [Action]
passage:
Sunday: Back from Madurai, everyone was cross. Ammamma had missed the temple she wanted, and Harsha's sister Diya had spent the trip in shops she hated. Harsha sat on the stairs for a long time.
Wednesday: Before the Puducherry trip, Harsha went to each person with a notebook. "Pick one place. Just one." Ammamma chose the old church by the sea, Amma the sunrise walk on the beach, his father Suraj the bakery lane, and Diya, after long thought, the botanical garden. Harsha fitted two into each day.
The next month: On the last evening in Puducherry, Diya was sketching leaves she had collected in the garden. Suraj bought everyone one more pastry, and Ammamma said, "This time everybody got a turn."

qa.q: Why did Harsha sit on the stairs after Madurai, and what might he have felt?
qa.a: Everyone had come back cross, so he probably felt troubled and wanted the next trip to be fairer.

qa.q: What else could Harsha try on a longer trip?
qa.a: Asking everyone for a first and second choice, so if one place is closed there is still something each person looks forward to.

qa.q: How did the plan look to Ammamma?
qa.a: Ammamma felt everybody got a turn, unlike Madurai when she missed her temple.

grounding: Across several weeks, a boy asks each family member to choose one place and builds the trip around their wishes so nobody feels ignored.
